claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a reported hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations.
Coupling machine-learning atomistic surrogates with continuum phase-field simulations will enable rapid prediction of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness in HfNbTiVAl10.
Explicit use of hierarchical-microstructure descriptors will improve prediction fidelity.
The proposed framework will reduce property-prediction error by approximately 50% relative to the stated baseline methods.
The proposed framework will reduce simulation runtime by approximately tenfold relative to the stated baseline methods.
Machine-learning models can compress high-fidelity atomistic information into efficient predictors of local elastic response.
Machine-learning models can compress high-fidelity atomistic information into efficient predictors of local plastic response.
Using surrogate predictions as spatially varying phase-field inputs will represent the effects of multilevel chemical fluctuations and phase-boundary distributions.
The integrated phase-field model can capture crack initiation and propagation relevant to toughness.
The integrated framework can retain essential mechanical physics while using substantially less computation.
The method is applicable from ambient to moderately elevated temperatures under quasi-static tensile and fracture loading.
Reliable application requires characterization of the spatial distribution of chemical fluctuations and phase-boundary characteristics.
Existing approaches do not explicitly account for the hierarchical structure.
Failure to account explicitly for the hierarchical structure contributes to high computational demands and less reliable toughness predictions.
The model may become unreliable if its descriptors omit secondary phases, defect concentrations, or other critical microstructural features.
The model may become unreliable at strain rates or temperatures far outside its calibration domain.
A blinded comparison against experimental measurements and baseline computational methods can test both predictive accuracy and computational efficiency.
Failure to achieve the specified accuracy improvement, runtime reduction, or 10% experimental-error criterion would refute the hypothesis.
